Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is it true or false? Any algorithm for sorting an array of size n must make at least Ω (n log n) comparisons.
Answer: FALSE. Any sorting algorithm that relies solely on comparisons must make at least Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. More generally, any sorting algorithm that can be modeled as a family of bounded-degree decision trees (or as a family of algebraic computation trees) requires at least Ω(n log n) operations in the worst case. But there are sorting algorithms that do not rely on comparisons (or other bounded-degree branches, or algebra) at all. The simplest of these algorithms is counting sort, which performs ZERO comparisons. Counting sort also runs in O(n) time, assuming we’re working in a model of computation that allows reading and writing input numbers in O(1) time. (If you’re not comfortable with that assumption, you’re going to have to work hard to justify comparing two input numbers in O(1) time.) Counting sort cannot be modeled as a bounded-degree decision tree, because it directly uses the data being sorted as indices into an array. If we work in the standard word RAM model, it is possible to sort n integers, each of which fits in a w-bit word, in O(nw) time using radix sort, or in O(n log w) time using van Emde Boas trees or fusion trees, or in O(n log log n) time using a complex algorithm of Yijie Han, or even in O(n) time if the word size w is sufficiently large. None of these algorithms work by performing one comparison at a time; the more efficient algorithms pack multiple integers into a single word, so that multiple comparisons can be performed in parallel using a single subtraction. The phrase “in the worst case” is also crucial; many sorting algorithms are faster when the input array is almost sorted. For example, if the index of each each element in the input array differs from its index in the output array by at most 10, then bubble sort ends after at most 10 passes, and thus sorts the array in only O(n) time.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: I started working on a systematic review paper and my research topic has changed halfway through, my supervisor still wants to me finish the paper that will not be used for my research, should I complete or challenge him?
Answer: I have two objections. First, the purpose of writing papers isn’t to help your own research; it’s to help other people’s research. Second, the skills you develop by writing a systematic review paper will be useful for your research, even if the review paper itself is not. You might consider having a discussion (not a “challenge”) with your advisor about whether the time you are spending developing long-term research skills by finishing the review paper might be better spent on short-term research goals more directly related to your thesis. Research requires all sort of strategic choices—for example, whether to focus on short-term versus long-term goals—between options that are sometimes at conflict. Part of your advisor’s job is to help you learn to navigate those choices, so it’s perfectly appropriate to ask them why they want you to finish the review paper, and how they expect that effort to impact progress toward your degree.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: Is there any website where I can publish my research paper for free (even if it's just online publication) and can give me a professional or official certification of publication?
Answer: I’ve never paid to publish anything, so… Any relevant journal or conference? Of course, the paper has to survive peer review (which takes anywhere from a few weeks to several months) before it is actually published. At least in computer science, legitimate venues do not charge authors to publish; in particular, legitimate open-access venues do not charge authors to publish open-access papers. Another possibility is arXiv or a similar preprint server. Papers on arXiv aren’t peer-reviewed (which misleads some people into thinking they’re not “published”), and they appear within 24 hours of submission. However, you do need to find a published researcher in your field to sponsor you if you haven’t posted on arXiv before. Whether the publication is “just online” or also on paper is utterly immaterial. To first approximation, nobody reads paper any more. Many long-standing journals still produce paper copies—mostly archival copies for libraries—but online-only journals are increasingly common. I don’t know what “a professional or official certification of publication” is. Most publication venues (including arXiv) indicate when the paper was submitted. The fact that the paper appears on the venue’s web site is concrete evidence that the paper is published, because “appears on the venue’s website” is the definition of “published by the venue”.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: So I have applied to a PhD program and I got accepted but I feel the supervisor is very impulsive from prior experience with students, for examples he has three DnF students in the past four years, what should I do to help me decide?
Answer: Talk with the supervisor’s current and former students, including at least one former student who left without a PhD. Directly. Without the supervisor present. In person if possible, and away from campus if possible. Look for patterns. Are the students comfortable talking about their supervisor? Are they generally happy (with their research, with their supervisor, with their environment, and with each other)? Are they successful (however you define success)? Are they getting the financial support, mentoring, and networking opportunities that they need? Are the supervisor’s expectations (for example, about research workload, collaboration, credit/authorship, writing, or thesis completion) clear and consistent and reasonable? For the former students who didn’t finish: Did they leave on good terms? Did the supervisor help them with their next steps? Then trust your gut. If something feels off, don’t accept the offer.

Name: Jeff Erickson
Question: What is the criteria for a PhD in computer science?
Answer: Exactly the same as the criteria for a PhD in every other field: Convince a committee of 3–5 experts that you have made a sufficiently novel and significant intellectual contribution to your field to deserve a PhD. There are usually a few other administrative hurdles along the way—classes, comprehensive / qualifying / candidacy / preliminary exams, thesis proposals, publications, conference presentations, teaching assistantships, writing and defending the actual thesis, etc.—but those are not the main criteria. At least in top computer science departments in the US, convincing the committee of experts usually requires the equivalent of 2 or 3 strong research publications, or 3–5 publications in strong venues, on a vaguely coherent topic. (No, those are not the same thing.) But “strong” and “equivalent” are subjective; the only people who can give you a definitive answer are your advisor and the other thesis committee members.
